title_zh: 转盘上的科里奥利效应
prompt_en:
A large flat turntable rotates counterclockwise on a lab bench. The table surface is marked with concentric circles and radial lines. At the center, a digital display shows the rotation speed and direction. Beside the turntable, an inclined ramp directs a ball from the edge toward the center. On the lab bench nearby, a whiteboard is divided into two sections: 'Rotating Frame' and 'Inertial Frame', with a table of coordinate axes and path descriptions. Text on digital rotation display reads exactly: "ω = 12.0 rpm | DIR: CCW
Angular velocity ω = 12.0 rpm = 1.26 rad/s. The Coriolis acceleration magnitude a_c = 2ωv, directed perpendicular to the velocity in the rotating frame. Derive from Newton's second law in a non-inertial frame: m a' = F - 2m ω × v' - m ω × (ω × r') - m α × r'.". Text on whiteboard (frame perspective section) reads exactly: "Rotating frame → curved path | Inertial frame → straight path
Rotating frame: the ball follows a curved path due to Coriolis force, which is fictitious. Inertial frame: the ball moves in a straight line; no force acts horizontally. This contrast proves that the apparent deflection is frame-dependent.". Text on whiteboard (coordinate table) reads exactly: "x-axis (inertial) | y-axis (inertial) | x' (rotating) | y' (rotating)
Path radius: r = 0.5 m; tangential speed v = ωr = 0.63 m/s". A ball is released from the edge by a lab assistant, rolling across the rotating turntable. Viewed from the rotating frame, the ball curves; a second observer just off the turntable watches the straight path in the inertial frame. They point at the whiteboard, discussing the observed paths and the non-existent centrifugal force in the inertial frame. The digital rotation display refreshes its readings while both observers note the contrasting trajectories.

Text in Journey board header reads exactly: "Journey board · Lisbon–Porto · 3 travelers · Jonas confirmed · group fare pending · Reserve group fare · Split 3 ways". prompt_en: Inside a warm kitchen while snow falls outside, the neighborhood mutual-aid board is projected onto one wall and mirrored on a tablet propped against a salt canister. The board shows a street map of the block with colored house icons, a column of typed resident requests, a volunteer route sign-up area, and a narrow community feed. A paper request card is attached at one address on the map; a clipboard beside the tablet records volunteer routes and their constraints; a system feed runs along the bottom; a small legend defines the icon colors. The teenager at the counter lifts an unassigned card from the request column, drags it over the map, and drops it when the route line snaps into place. The card then flips to an assigned state with her name and a countdown, the resident’s icon changes color, and the feed posts a system confirmation of the action. Text in paper request card pinned beside the Maple Street marker reads exactly: "Maple St, 4:30pm - Sidewalk and front steps need clearing after the storm. I can leave the key under the blue pot if you need the back entry, but please knock twice before you start. Mrs. Okonkwo, 34 Maple.". Text in volunteer route sign-up list on the clipboard reads exactly: "Route 3: 46 Cedar (M. Ruiz), 12 Birch (J. Lin), 34 Maple (open). Bring shovel and salt bag; 46 Cedar has extra de-icer. If 34 Maple is assigned, skip it unless snow exceeds 4 inches.". Text in community feed system message reads exactly: "System 4:12 PM - 34 Maple claimed by A. Park. She will knock twice and use the blue-pot key. Route 3 de-icer from 46 Cedar moved to 12 Birch while she covers Maple St.". Text in map legend panel reads exactly: "Legend: red = requested, orange = claimed, green = done. Snow depth 3 in.". Text in claimed status badge on the dragged request card reads exactly: "A. Park · ETA 4:30 · 17 min left". The teenager drags the request card from the resident-help column onto her planned route line on the map and releases it. As a result, the card updates to show her name and a countdown, the map icon for that address turns from red to orange, and the community feed adds a system message saying the task is now assigned. In the route sign-up area, the prior open slot is replaced by her name, and a route note is adjusted so no other volunteer’s path overlaps that stop. Ensure all text is crisp, legible, and high-contrast. The clipboard is a distinct physical object separate from the projected board.

Text in dispatcher reroute brief reads exactly: "Cell MB-7 tops FL380 and blocks the planned MSP route. Text in fuel summary card reads exactly: "Trip 19,550 lb · Contingency 1,200 · Reserve 5,400 · Arrival 6,700 OK". Text in route comparison table reads exactly: "PLAN J80  1,712 nmi  18,400 lb  08:45  |  PROPOSED VIA BIL  1,748 nmi  19,550 lb  08:56". Text in captain reply bubble reads exactly: "Okafor: Recleared via BIL. Will watch cell tops and report.". The pilot opens the fuel summary, expands the reserve bar until it shows a safe margin, then taps an accept control on the reply card; the route strip switches from a proposed state to a cleared state.

The display has a header bar, rooftop-generation gauges for each house, a live tariff ticker, a bid board where solar owners post surplus energy, and a graph of transferred energy. A side manager console shows settlement records and grid-load flags. A solar owner taps the bid board and raises the ask on her surplus, and a renter across the room accepts it. The mediator adjusts the accepted ask as the tariff trends upward, the transfer graph gains a new bar, an inbox notice appears for both households, and the console logs the settlement with a grid-load note. Text in wall-screen display header reads exactly: "Copperline Community Energy Market — Block 6 Live". Text in bid board region reads exactly: "Offer #8 from 14 Chestnut has 14 kWh surplus at 0.19/kWh, firm until 16:10. The renter bid 0.15 for 12 kWh. Text in transfer-graph summary panel reads exactly: "Transferred today 42.7 kWh across 48 transfers. Peak 3.2 kW at 14:05. Street load 91%, next 15 min forecast down. Median accepted spread 0.04.". Text in settlement manager console reads exactly: "Settlement 104: 14 Chestnut matched 22 Poplar. 12 kWh settled at 0.19/kWh. Meter delta agrees 12.01 kWh. Grid load flag H2; area cap not exceeded.". Text in household inbox notice reads exactly: "Your 12 kWh purchase at 0.19/kWh cleared 16:04. Credit 2.28.". The solar owner raises her ask after seeing the afternoon cloud edge form; the renter accepts; the mediator adjusts the accepted ask as the tariff trends upward, filling a new bar in the transfer graph and updating the settlement console.

The colony card is divided into three vertical sections: top is the 'Feeding Log Table', middle is the 'Supply Request Panel', and bottom is the 'Volunteer Group Thread'. A 'Clinic Alert Feed' runs as a sidebar on the far left of the screen. A volunteer in a hooded sweatshirt interacts with the screen. Text in the veterinary alert feed post reads exactly: "Clinic alert for C-14 Riverside Park. Upper respiratory infection suspected: two adults and one kitten have crusted eyes and sneezing. Clean bowls daily; add L-lysine to wet food for 7 days. If appetite drops, mark the pin as urgent and call 555-014-2271.". Text in the feeding log table on the colony card reads exactly: "Route C-14: Mon fed, Tue fed, Wed missed, Thu fed, Fri fed 7:42 AM. Last fed 07:42, next check 19:00, bowls rinsed, kitten appetite normal.". Text in the supply request board auto-suggest panel reads exactly: "Suggested C-14 order: 2 extra wet food tins, 1 L-lysine, 1 paper bowl pack. Reason: URI watch active. Confirm order?". Text in the volunteer group thread missed-day alert reads exactly: "C-14 missed Wednesday feeding. Please double-check tonight. Maya will cover at 7 PM.". Text in the map pin watch badge reads exactly: "C-14 Riverside Park · watch · URI". The scene shows a caretaker tapping the feeding checkmark, updating the log timestamp and sending a missed-day warning into the volunteer thread. A second volunteer applies the watch badge to the alerted colony pin; the map badge changes, the supply suggestion adds the health-related items, and the same colony identifier is shown in the pin, log, alert, and order panel.

The display shows a digital twin of stacked rack rows represented as color-coded blocks; one block is highlighted and edged in amber. Through a glass wall behind the display, actual basil tiers are visible with lower leaves yellowing on a selectable rack. The display is organized into distinct panels for clarity. On the left, a large 'Agronomy Note' panel reads exactly: "PhytoPlex — Zone 4 Agronomy Note: Lower leaves show interveinal chlorosis, young leaves show edge burn, and no pests are visible. pH 6.9 and EC 1.6 mS/cm point to line 2 blockage for 18 h, limiting iron and calcium uptake. Below the note, a 'Zone 4 history' table reads exactly: "Week 21 transplant • Week 22 tip burn • Week 23 chlorosis • Week 24 recovery test". To the right of the note, a 'Sensor trend' card with a real-time line graph reads exactly: "EC 1.6 → 2.2 mS/cm • pH 6.9 → 5.8 • DO 7.1 mg/L • VPD 0.8 kPa • Root temp 23.4°C". A grower in a blue apron presses the amber-highlighted block, then drags a 24-hour trace on the sensor trend card. prompt_en: In a wood-panelled museum research room at dusk, two curators and one community representative gather before a large wall screen. On the right side is the 'Decision Card'. Beneath the left and center panels runs the 'Custody Timeline' strip. Papers and a tea cup rest on the table below. The text in the center historical note panel reads exactly: "Collected at Ouidah in 1892 by trader Félix Sohier after a fire. Kpóssi memory: hidden in a shrine, not sold. The 1898 register says 'donation' with no donor; no receipt or deed survives. Written record and oral memory diverge — custody remains incomplete.". The text in the left object dossier card reads exactly: "Object 1898.12.7 | Brass figure, Fon people | Provenance: Ouidah, Dahomey | Sources: Fonds Sohier 12J/7; Ouidah ledger folio 23; Kpóssi interview, 2023". The text in the timeline strip beneath the dossier reads exactly: "Custody timeline: 1892 fire — removed (unverified); 1897 'curiosities' (disputed); 1898 donation, no donor; 2024 review opened.". The text in the decision card at the right edge reads exactly: "Access: community view only; repatriation dossier restricted. Next step: Kpóssi family delegates inspect the figure in person; museum responds by 31 Mar.". One curator points to the historical note in the center. The community representative looks at the timeline at the bottom. A second curator marks a checkbox on the decision card on the right and writes in a notebook.

title_en: Kelpway Berth Control — MN308 Recovery Handoff
title_zh: 凯尔普威泊位控制 — MN308 恢复交接
prompt_en: In the glass control tower of Kelpway Terminal, dawn light over a container yard. A large, wall-mounted berth coordination console dominates the view, divided into three distinct panels and a bottom strip. The left panel is a white paper note titled 'MN308 handoff'. The center panel is a digital screen showing a berth schedule. The right panel is a digital screen showing a priority list. A terminal shift manager, crane coordinator, and rail planner stand beside the console; the manager's hand rests on a trackpad, and the rail planner holds a clipboard. Text in the left-hand handoff panel reads exactly: "MN308 handoff: Vessel lost 3h to weather; plan Berth 7 06:00–14:00, requires +1.2m tide window. 430 import empties must reach rail ramp by 18:00. Available labor 18 gangs, below cap of 22; swap two tug jobs to 04:30 reduces berth idle. Conflict: reefer bank at Berth 9 demands shore power at 05:00, so yard shuttle drops from 8 to 5 loops. Accepted plan keeps MN308 on priority and rechecks rail after 12:00.". Text in the center berth sequence table reads exactly: "Berth 7: MN308 06:00–14:00; Berth 9: reefer bank 05:00–09:00; Berth 4: tug layup 04:30; Berth 12: rail transfer 14:00–18:00.". Text in the right-side container priority list reads exactly: "Priority A: MN308 reefers 42; Priority B: export dry 1,180; Priority C: import empties 430; rail cutoff 18:00.". Text in the lower tide and labor constraint strip on the console reads exactly: "Tide window: +1.2m at 06:00, +0.8m at 10:00; labor 18 of 22 gangs; overtime allowed after 16:00; rail ramp capacity 5 loops per hour.". Text in the top alert banner reads exactly: "Warning: Reefer power conflict at Berth 9; two tug jobs moved to 04:30; plan accepted.". The manager drags the two tug job blocks earlier; the top alert banner flares amber and the shuttle counter drops several loops. prompt_en: A large remote-classroom interface fills the screen. The deaf instructor signs in a central video tile while the interpreter appears in a smaller adjacent tile. Around the video area, distinct panes show the lesson explanation, a question queue, a pinned term board, and a transcript correction log. Student video tiles line the bottom edge, with one student's name highlighted in the queue. Text in Top navigation bar reads exactly: "Handspan Live — ASL 201: Classifiers in Motion". Text in Main lesson pane reads exactly: "Classifier predicates combine a handshape and a movement path. In the clip, the 3-handshape on the right edge represents the car; the arc down the slope is the hill. The handshape does not name the car again — it tracks its location. When the car leaves the road and overturns, use the bent-V handshape to show the vehicle rotated. This is why we read direction of movement before meaning of the sign.". Text in Interpreter note strip reads exactly: "Interpreter note: at 04:12, 'SHE WALKED-PAST' uses a slow 1-handshape arc. I chose 'she strolled by' because the visible effort is relaxed, not hurried.". Text in Ask queue panel reads exactly: "Ask queue — Aisha: eye gaze question; Raj: vehicle classifier; Mei: Why does GIVE start near the chest?; Leo: resolved — direction marks subject/object.". Text in Pinned terminology board reads exactly: "Pinned terms: CL:3 vehicle; CL:V overturned; path movement; role shift; eye gaze; non-manual marker.". Text in Transcript correction log reads exactly: "Auto-caption: he give book. Correction: HE GAVE-BOOK — verb moves from giver to receiver.". The instructor stops the playback clip, points to a handshape diagram, and repeats the classifier shape. The interpreter types a note and updates the translation. A corrected caption line replaces the auto-caption. In the queue, Mei's question card moves to the top, then Leo marks his card as resolved after the instructor responds.

Around the table, three residents and two architects point at the model; one resident holds a laser rangefinder. Text in wall screen, resident concern panel reads exactly: "From Unit 3C: the east room darkens by 14:30 in March. We want the bench line visible from the kitchen window. title_en: Nereid Light – Oxygen Shadow Zone at Station 12
prompt_en: On the bridge of the research vessel Nereid Light, the TidePilot console is a wide, single operational surface. On the far left, a large screen displays a station map with a drawn transect. The map overlay text reads exactly: "STN-12 · 47.2°N 129.8°W · Cast 3 · transect 5/14 · bottom 2,970 m". Next to the map, a screen shows a depth-oxygen graph updating continuously. In the center, a large panel displays the open bridge log. The text in this panel reads exactly: "Oxygen at 850 m remains below 8 µmol/kg despite two casts; the station-12 profile shows an expanding shadow zone. We keep the 22-bottle rosette sequence but extend the 1,500 m Niskin hold for methane duplicates, unless the 23:00 threshold forces a trimmed cast.". To the right of the log, a vertical 'Live CTD' card displays real-time data. On the far right, a 'Weather constraint card' is visible with text reading exactly: "Wind NW 28 kt · seas 2.8 m · deck safe until 23:00 · abandon below 1,200 m if roll >4°". The operator watches the real-time graph as the depth trace climbs past 1,480 m and the oxygen curve flattens near its low value. Bottle icons light up in sequence while a completion counter ticks forward. A cursor moves through the log panel, selects the last sentence, and then taps a confirm button. The weather card simultaneously highlights a cutoff time and a roll limit in amber.

title_zh: Signalpost 核实台——Riverline 大桥说法
prompt_en: A newsroom verification desk where a reporter and an editor inspect a wide source-comparison workspace. The screen is split into a left column for evidence and provenance, a right column for quote comparison and a decision lane, and a bottom strip for the timeline. An open file folder and a printed press release lie on the desk, but all working text appears on the display. Text in Screen header reads exactly: "Signalpost Verify · Claim #RB-0418 · Status: in verification". Text in Evidence memo panel reads exactly: "Claim under review: City Press Office says Riverline Bridge repairs finished 11 days early and $318,000 under its $2.1M budget. Three independent sources agree on final cost $1.79M, but the award ledger records a $140K change order for night waterproofing and the original completion clause allowed weather days. The early-finish date is contradicted by two delivery logs: the last concrete pour was May 2, while the project closeout was signed May 14. The under-budget figure is therefore defensible; the early-completion claim is not.". Text in Source provenance row reads exactly: "Source records: Procurement Ledger 2024-118 (pages 4, 12), delivery ticket #B-1142, weather log May 1–14, press office release PR-4023. Uploaded by L. Nwosu; county export hash verified.". Text in Quote comparison column reads exactly: "Press Office: 'completed ahead of schedule and well under cost' — Contractor daily log: 'final pour May 2; punch list closed May 14' — Discrepancy: 12 calendar days.". Text in Timeline strip reads exactly: "Apr 18 night waterproofing change order signed · May 2 final concrete pour · May 3 press release posted · May 14 closeout signed". Text in Editorial decision sticky reads exactly: "Editor Q: Is 'under budget' still safe if the $140K night waterproofing change order is reported? Reply by 15:30. Decision: keep under-budget angle; drop early-completion phrase.". The reporter selects a discrepancy icon beside the paired quotations. The interface highlights the conflicting dates and draws a red connection between the press-release row and the delivery-log row; the editor’s sticky note then rises to the top of the decision lane while the workspace header remains in the verification state.

title_zh: 日晷种子公社：为归还批次的重新评级
prompt_en: At a long table in a gardening cooperative's tool shed, a coordinator works at a desktop computer. The screen shows a seed-lending web app with four linked regions: a return log on the left, an inventory detail panel in the center, a member request queue on the right, and a branch-transfer strip at the bottom. A returned seed packet lies beside the keyboard in an open storage box, and a courier route sheet is clipped to the box. Text in Return-log card in the seed-library desktop app reads exactly: "Return R-311: Glass Gem corn, lot GG-2024. Packet returned 04-28; 14 seeds remain. Germination check: 2 of 10 sown seeds grew. Condition: low germination — re-rate before next loan.". Text in Inventory detail panel for the variety reads exactly: "Inventory: Glass Gem corn, lot GG-2024. Rating: 3.1/5 (was 4.6/5). Available: 2 packets. Last germination 04-24: 40%. Policy: rating below 3.5 moves lot to Needs Replenishment automatically.". Text in Request queue entry from a member farm reads exactly: "Request Q-884: Cedar Row Farm (M. Okafor) wants 2 packets of Glass Gem corn, lot GG-2024 or newer, for a 1/4-acre plot; pickup May 10; note: cold soil hurt last year's stand — prefers early-planting seed.". Text in Branch-transfer strip at the bottom of the app reads exactly: "Transfer: 1 backup packet GG-2024 from Sundial shelf B-2 to Cedar Row Farm; Tuesday courier; approved Lin M.; source 2023 germ 96%.". The coordinator reads the return-log evidence about poor germination, then lowers the variety's rating in the inventory detail panel. The rating change instantly moves the lot into a restocking state while the waiting farm request remains visible. The coordinator approves a transfer from another branch, and the backup packet's source and courier route appear in the transfer strip, satisfying the request.

prompt_en:

1. Top Left: A gameplay video window showing a racing game with a car on a track.
2. Top Right: A 'Case Summary Panel' containing the exact text: "Case #8921: Runner 'Velo' claims WR on 'Neon Drift'. Dispute: 12.4s pause at Sector 4. Runner states: 'Controller disconnected, forced reset. No save/load. Pure input gap.' Evidence: Raw input log shows zero activity for 12.4s. Video shows static screen. Request: Verify with time adjustment or reject."
3. Middle Left: A 'Rule Citation & Exception Module' containing the exact text: "Rule 4.2: 'Interruptions due to hardware failure are permitted if no progress is lost.' Exception 4.2-B: 'Pauses >10s require proof of no save/load. Time penalty: +5s added to final time.'"
4. Middle Right: A 'Moderator Ruling Draft Box' containing the exact text: "Ruling: Verified. The 12.4s pause aligns with hardware reset. No save/load detected. Applying Exception 4.2-B. Final time adjusted: 14:02.4 + 5.0s = 14:07.4. Status: Accepted."
5. Bottom Center: A prominent blue button with the exact text: "Publish Ruling to Leaderboard".

The interface is designed for clarity, with high-contrast text. Ensure all text is spelled correctly and clearly legible.

prompt_en: In a bright neighborhood center, a waist-height interactive table glows with a simplified district map. On the left side of the table, a large white card displays clear, legible text: "Proposal 14: Shade Canopies on Market Street. Summer surface temps reached 41°C on the playground side, so three tensile canopies over the west seating row would lower peak heat by 6-8°C. Estimated cost $38,000, covering 11 trees, 8 benches, and 2 drinking fountains. The cost includes installation and maintenance for five years; if funded before June, installation can happen before the July heat wave.". Directly below this card, a smaller white card shows a cost table with clear text: "Shade canopies $38,000 | Crosswalk signals $24,500 | Library Sunday hours $31,500 | Total requested $94,000 | Cap $90,000". To the right of the proposal card, a pinned white note reads clearly: "Equity note: Block 2 has 73% children under 12 and no shaded playground; Block 5 has 82% residents without cars and the widest crossing gaps. Families in both blocks report avoiding summer midday walks.". In the center of the table, a circular allocation ring displays clear text: "Agreed split: Shade $36,000, Crosswalks $24,500, Library $29,500. Total $90,000. Consensus reached — 6 of 7 blocks approve, one abstains.". On the far right, a yellow sticky note reads clearly: "Counter: Sunday library hours serve 1,200 weekly visitors across all ages, while shade helps roughly 400 daily playground users. Can we trim canopy cloth and add one Sunday per month instead?". A group of residents of different ages leans around the table. One resident drags a shaded-tree token from the proposal card toward the center; the central ring rotates, reducing the shade segment and expanding the library segment. Other residents nod as a green checkmark appears in the ring's center.

prompt_en: A high-resolution, wide shot of a family archive restoration workspace. The scene is warmly lit. In the center, a large wooden worktable holds a tri-fold archival display board. On the left panel of the board, a large, clear note titled 'Marta's Memory' reads exactly: "Marta's memory: The Voss family picnic at Clear Lake, September 1962. Aunt Ines had just returned from Montreal, so she wore the yellow dress. Uncle Theo was still upset about the tractor loan and stayed near the grill. The dog Taffy knocked over the lemonade. The man with the camera was the neighbor from the lumber mill, whose name I think began with M. I remember it was his last summer at the lake.". In the center panel, a damaged group photo is displayed. To the right of the photo, a 'Date Evidence Card' reads exactly: "Photograph back: “Voss picnic, summer 1961”. Film box: Kodak 5293, expires Dec 1962. Marta’s note: September 1962. Local weather log: Sept 24 1962 clear and 76°F. Decision: use 1962-09-24.". Below the date card, a 'Face Annotation List' reads exactly: "A: Ines Voss, 24. B: Theo Voss, 38. C: unknown man, maybe neighbor. D: Taffy, dog. Note: Marta says C worked at the lumber mill and had red hair; D is the same dog in the 1960 Christmas photo.". On the right panel of the board, a 'Scan Treatment Log' reads exactly: "Scan date: 2024-05-12. Scanner: Alvarez. Repair: scratch removal pass 2; tear patch from negative plate 7; color matching with original print. Next step: review top-left edge.". Below the log, a 'Consent Setting' card reads exactly: "Share with: descendants of Voss siblings. Status: approved by submitter. Access: not public.". At the bottom right, a 'Resolved Catalog Record' reads exactly: "Catalog record: 1962-09-24 Clear Lake Picnic. Owner: Voss Family. Location: Box 14, Folder 3. Subjects: picnic, dog, yellow dress, neighbor. Restored by: L. Alvarez.". Surrounding the board are cotton gloves, a magnifier, and stacked photo boxes. The text on all cards is sharp, legible, and correctly spelled.

title_zh: 国际象棋比赛仲裁员控制台：争议结果审查
prompt_en:
A dedicated arbiter console for an international chess tournament is active in a quiet officials' room. The main screen is divided into several connected panels. On the left, a digital pairing table lists recent board assignments with player names, federations, and result flags. A center evidence pane displays a board diagram with a highlighted endgame position, a move notation line, and a clock-time graph annotated with critical timestamps. To the right, a rulings discussion thread scrolls with official comments. The console shows real-time tournament data and a pending review marker for a disputed result. The interface is clean, dense with information, and clearly part of a professional arbiter's workflow. Text in evidence pane header reads exactly: "Evidence: Board 7 - Carlsen vs Nakamura - Round 9 - disputed result; marker: flag fell after black's 41st move.". Text in chess board diagram labels reads exactly: "Position after 41...Nf6+ - Black's clock: 00:00 - White's clock: 03:12 - Flag fell at 00:00; per FIDE 6.9, game drawn if flag fall preceded checkmate.
Evidence pane note: Position after 41...Nf6+. Black's clock shows 00:00 at move completion, flag fell at 00:00. White's clock had 03:12 remaining. Per FIDE article 6.9, if a player's flag falls before checkmate is delivered, the game is drawn if the opponent cannot checkmate by any possible series of legal moves. Here, black's flag fell, but white has insufficient mating material (only a king and two knights), so the result is a draw.". Text in ruling discussion thread reads exactly: "Arbiter Chen: Flag fell after black's 41st move; per FIDE 6.9, game is drawn. Nakamura's appeal pending. Awaiting claim verification.". An arbiter sits at the console, carefully reviewing the pairing table, the evidence pane, and the ruling discussion thread. The arbiter clicks on the highlighted disputed game, bringing up the full move notation and both players' clock records, and marks a critical time-out with an annotation tool on the screen. After cross-referencing the clock graph, the arbiter types a short ruling explanation into the discussion thread and clicks the 'Submit Preliminary Ruling' button. The console interface responds quickly, with all information presented in a professional tournament-management style, conveying a concentrated and tense atmosphere.

title_en: Aida's Table: The Recipe That Crossed the Sea
title_zh: 艾达的餐桌：一张飘洋过海的食谱
prompt_en: Three relatives—an older woman, her adult niece, and a teenager—stand close around a worn wooden kitchen table. On it lie a stained handwritten recipe sheet, an airmail letter, a brown paper scrap, an open cookbook, a bowl of canned fish, potatoes, onions, lemons, bay leaves, and capers. The older woman turns the recipe sheet toward the lamp; the adult niece unfolds the letter; the teenager balances a pencil over the cookbook page. Text on worn recipe card, creased and speckled with dried dough, handwritten in blue ink reads exactly: "Baked Fish for a Small Kitchen. From Aida's house, 1962. 3 potatoes, thinly sliced. 1 onion, chopped small. 1 can pink salmon. oil, salt, pepper, paprika. Bake covered forty minutes. Do not add tomatoes; your father once did and it turned sour. Serve with cabbage and dark bread.". Text on thin airmail sheet, folded into thirds, typed reads exactly: "Your sister, 1974. Dear Aida, the fish seller had no salmon, so I took smoked whitefish and added one bay leaf. I baked it thirty minutes, not forty. The children ate it twice. Do not worry about the tomatoes. The coast is cold; we use what the boat brings. — Mara". Text on scrap of brown paper bag, pencil handwriting reads exactly: "Tuesday. Market M.: no pink salmon. Take canned mackerel and a lemon. It will do. — M.". Text on first page of a spiral-bound family cookbook, marker and ink reads exactly: "Aida's Mackerel, as the family makes it now. Salmon or mackerel, one bay leaf, thirty minutes covered. We add capers and lemon. This is the new year table version, made for Izzy's first meal. Keep the card, Mara's letter, and the market note beside it.". The older woman reads the handwritten recipe, then points to the letter. The niece slides the market scrap next to the recipe sheet and lifts a can of fish. The teenager writes a new version into the cookbook, then lays all four texts side by side on the table.

scene_type: jazz ensemble rehearses an inherited arrangement
title_en: The River Still Moves: Rehearsing Delia's Year
title_zh: 河仍在流动：排练迪莉娅之年
prompt_en: In a lamplit rehearsal room, four jazz players sit in a loose arc around music stands, while the bandleader leans over the piano score. The trumpet player lifts a mute away from the bell, the bassist sustains a low D, and the pianist spreads a chord. The bandleader taps a handwritten note, then a folded half-sheet letter, then points to the set list; the ensemble resumes and plays the opening with a quieter grief. Text on handwritten rehearsal note taped to the bandleader's score reads exactly: "For Delia's year we begin as lament but we do not stay there. At bar 47 the melody stands open, no hat, no mute. This is not forgetting the rain; it is how the river keeps the rain and still moves. — Etta". Text on bandleader's half-sheet rehearsal letter reads exactly: "Tonight we honor the written lament, then the horns will revoice the last A together. Nobody gets erased. We change how grief is carried.". Text on chord chart with pencil annotation reads exactly: "47: open voicing — bass sustains D, piano leaves the blue notes until the ensemble breathes.". Text on set list propped on the piano reads exactly: "Set 1: Blue Meridian (lament revoiced) / Cedar Walk / Delia's Year". Following the written order, the players trace from the original note to the chord chart; when the bandleader confirms, the horns take out their mutes, the piano changes to an open voicing, and the drummer broadens the time. The group plays the passage again together, softer and unburdened.

prompt_en:
In a sunlit cooperative pottery studio, members gather around a cooling kiln shelf holding several identical stoneware cups. An older potter holds a clay-recipe notebook open to a page detailing a specific iron-rich glaze formula. A younger member points to a handwritten kiln shelf map showing position codes. A small white tag on one cup reads 'Anonymous'. Hands rotate the cups, examining incised marks on the foot rings against the notebook's notes. The group discusses the evidence, referencing the map and the glaze test results recorded in the notebook. They agree on the attribution based on the unique scar pattern and glaze composition. Finally, they sign a separate correction slip and replace the anonymous tag with a new label crediting the makers. 

Text on Clay-recipe notebook page reads exactly: "Batch 44: High-iron slip, 1200C. Note: Only Mara and Eli used this mix. Look for the triple-slash scar on the foot ring, left side. Glaze runs slightly thick near the handle."

Text on Handwritten kiln shelf map reads exactly: "Shelf 3, Pos 7-9: Mara/Eli joint load. Glaze test #44. Warning: Do not stack. These cups are fragile. Check for the scar mark before sale."

Text on Original anonymous tag on cup reads exactly: "Anonymous. Studio Collective. $12."

Text on Correction slip signed by group reads exactly: "Attribution Correction: Cups from Shelf 3, Pos 7-9 are by Mara and Eli. Verified by glaze batch 44 and foot-ring scar. Signed: J., K., M., E."

Text on New attribution label reads exactly: "Mara & Eli. Joint Work. Batch 44."

Hands rotate the cups to inspect foot-ring incisions, compare them with the notebook's glaze formula and the shelf map's position codes, discuss the findings, sign the correction slip, and replace the anonymous tag with the agreed attribution label.

scene_type: neighborhood mural reveals a changing civic poem
prompt_en: In a narrow alley shaded by laundry lines, a tall brick wall carries a mural built up from pale blue and ochre paint layers. A ladder leans against the wall. An older woman in paint-spattered overalls, the mural's original painter, and a younger resident sponge a pale blue section with water. As the paint softens, faded ochre lines appear beneath. A small metal plaque is bolted beside the drainpipe, and sprayed lines cover part of the upper blue layer. Text on painted ochre lines on the exposed lower wall reads exactly: "We counted stairs in the dark / and knew the mill whistle by heart. / When the gate closed we wrote our names in chalk / so the wall would not lose us. / Old wall, hold the door.". Text on painted service plaque beside the drainpipe reads exactly: "Repainted 1998 by E. Voss. Graffiti removed 2009; poem kept. Cleaned with soft cloth, 2019.". Text on spray-painted lines on the upper blue layer reads exactly: "They say the hill changed. We are the hill now. / Our names are on the market receipt, not chalk. / The stairs still creak for anyone who listens.". Text on hand-painted dedication in the mural's lower corner reads exactly: "La Loma Mural — first painted 1987 by A. Rivas.". The older woman wipes the pale blue paint until an ochre line appears, then stops and reads it aloud to the younger resident. He climbs the ladder with a damp cloth and uncovers the upper stanza. A third neighbor points to the plaque beneath the drainpipe and then up to the sprayed lines. The two cleaners pause at the edge of the original poem so the earlier and newer writings remain visible together.

prompt_en: In a modest workshop room, three translators sit at a long wooden table covered with dictionaries, coffee cups, pencils and collated pages. On the wall in front of them, a sepia source-poem card is pinned at the center; to its left and right hang two typed translations, and a handwritten rationale note is pinned beneath them. A small yellow sticky note rests on the table between the two translation sheets. Text on sepia ink card pinned at the center of the wall reads exactly: "En el umbral, luz que heredamos, menos que el polvo; abre la puerta, mira el camino, cada paso vuelve a empezar.". Text on typed sheet to the left of the source card reads exactly: "At the threshold, the light we inherit is less than dust; open the door, look at the road, each step begins again.". Text on typed sheet to the right of the source card reads exactly: "On the doorstep, inherited light weighs no more than dust; open the door, watch the road, every step starts over.". Text on handwritten rationale note pinned below the translations reads exactly: "Fuller smooths the rhythm; Reza keeps 'doorstep' and 'inherited' for closeness. We debate whether 'polvo' means dust as absence or dust as daily work.". Text on small yellow sticky note on the table between the two typed sheets reads exactly: "we carry the light; each step begins again". Two translators lean toward the center card, tracing the source lines with a pencil, then alternate pointing to the translation on the left and the one on the right. The third translator reads the rationale note aloud and nods. After a moment of debate, the workshop coordinator lifts the sticky note from the table and places it directly between the two typed translations; one translator smiles, while the other picks up a pencil and makes a small correction beside the revised line.

prompt_en: A historic cemetery on a breezy hill. At one weathered headstone, a conservator in a beige work apron kneels on a padded mat, smoothing acid-free paper over the carved face and rubbing it with a wax crayon. Beside her, an assistant holds open a heavy burial ledger. On a portable research board, a handwritten letter and a note card are clipped, and a small green conservation stake stands at the grave. Text on weathered headstone in Rowan Hill Cemetery reads exactly: "EMILIA ROSS · KEEPER OF THE TIDE CLOCK · STILLED ONLY AT THE LAST BELL · AGED 65 YEARS · THE HARBOR KNEW HER HOURS". Text on open burial ledger reads exactly: "PLOT 27 · EMILIA ROSS · DIED 19 APRIL 1906 · AGE 65 · HEART FAILURE · STONE SET 1907 · DAUGHTER M. HALE". Text on letter clipped to research board reads exactly: "Dear Archivist, my great-aunt tended the harbor clock for forty years. The stone says tide keeper; the ledger may set it right.". Text on note card clipped to research board reads exactly: "Rubbing supports only EMILIA ROSS. Ledger records 'harbor clock' on the old pier. No source calls her tide keeper; treat as dedication, not occupation.". Text on small green conservation stake at grave reads exactly: "ROWAN HILL CEMETERY CONSERVATION · EMILIA ROSS · PLOT 27". The conservator pulls the rubbing paper taut, letting worn letters darken on the page. The assistant angles the ledger toward the light, then taps a line with a gloved finger. The conservator compares the stone, the ledger, and the letter, then writes a careful line on the note card, separating the epitaph's poetic phrase from documented fact.

prompt_en: In a community-center hallway with cinder-block walls, three volunteers sort materials from a department store that closed decades ago. On a folding table, employee name badges with stenciled department codes lie beside receipts paper-clipped to handwritten oral-history cards. A faded newspaper clipping is taped to the wall. One volunteer sorts the badges while another writes an index-card timeline. Text on handwritten oral-history card reads exactly: "Aug 17, 1963: LeRoy and I sat down. Manager said closed; white customers got coffee. Police came at 12:30, no arrests. Iced tea never came.". Text on faded newspaper clipping taped to the wall reads exactly: "SIT-IN CLOSES COUNTER / Aug 17, 1963. Employees denied service refused to leave. Manager cited repairs. Text on index-card timeline being written by a volunteer reads exactly: "11:20 AM Clara and LeRoy sit. / 12:15 PM receipt refused. / 12:30 PM police, no arrests. / 1:05 PM counter closed. / Badge 27 = C. Simmons.". Text on employee name badge reads exactly: "SIMMONS, C. / DEPT. 27 / LUNCH COUNTER / 108". A volunteer matches each employee badge code to a name on an oral-history card, then writes a timeline index card that places the named workers at the lunch counter on the day of the demonstration. She compares the lunch-counter receipt with the testimony, checks the department codes, and clips the finished timeline card to the display. The receipt is clearly visible on the table, distinct from the wall clippings. The timeline card is the focus of the writing action, with clear, legible text. The badge text is sharp and readable.

prompt_en: The independent print room is warm with ink and daylight. Text on front cover riso proof reads exactly: "Keepers of the Arcade — Issue 13". Text on center spread testimony page reads exactly: "I was nine when the first arcade roof went on. Vendors slept under the stalls with baskets. The official history counts rents; it hides the hands that painted the shutters.". Text on tipped correction strip on galley proof reads exactly: "Correction to Issue 12: the vinegar stall belonged to Wen Hsiu-Ling, not Wen Rung-Fa. Source: Mei Lan.". Text on editorial statement page reads exactly: "The issue prints the east market as its residents speak it, not as the archive lists it. Each voice was read back before printing.". Text on colophon page reads exactly: "Printed in 400 copies on leftover stock. Drawings are from market visits. Type set by hand.". One volunteer places a correction slip over the attributed name on a galley proof; another turns the slip so the older woman can read it. The market vendor nods and initials the editorial statement page with a pencil. The printer operator pulls the drum guard aside and runs a single test sheet through the risograph.

title_en: A Name Under the Forest Floor
prompt_en:
In the lofty restoration workshop of a small repertory theatre, an enormous hand-painted woodland backdrop lies flat on the floor, its linen surface held taut by wooden battens and felt pads. Conservators in aprons kneel on rolling boards, working with cotton swabs and solvent around the painted trees and undergrowth. On a wheeled trolley at the edge are aged paper inventory records, small tins of paint samples with tie-on labels, and a fresh sheet of paper clipped to a wooden board. Text on handwritten note and signature exposed under overpaint in the lower right corner of the backdrop reads exactly: "With M. Delacroix for the crown and sky, I, W. N. Lane, painted the glades and leaf work. A. Voss cut in the birch trunks. The stage manager asked us to keep our names from the playbill.". Text on aged production inventory card on the restoration trolley reads exactly: "1937 Inventory
Riverside Repertory
Hamlet, Act 4
Forest and Glade
Scenery painted by M. Delacroix
Costumes S. Feld
Lighting R. Kim". Text on tie-on labels on small pigment sample tins reads exactly: "L-4 emerald green over lead white, crown. L-7 ochre and burnt umber, glade. L-12 iron black under resin brown, birch.". Text on new attribution sheet clipped to a board on the trolley reads exactly: "Attribution corrected 2024. M. Delacroix composed the design; W. N. Lane and A. Voss executed the glades and woodland floor.". A conservator wets a swab at the lower right area of the drop and slowly rubs the grimy overpaint. Beneath it, handwriting emerges with a signature. She pauses, uses a clean cloth to soften the area, then reads the revealed lines aloud to a colleague. Her colleague lifts the inventory card, matches the single credit against the hidden statement, and carries both to the trolley. He picks up the corrected attribution sheet, adds a date, and slides it into the production record binder.

scene_type: tattoo motif consent and lineage consultation
prompt_en:
In a quiet tattoo studio, a client, their aunt, and an artist gather around a drafting table. They examine a sketchbook containing a family crest, a tracing overlay with red annotations, a consent worksheet, and a final stencil label. The artist uses a pen to cross out a symbol on the overlay and redraws a border line. The aunt and client review the changes and prepare to sign the document. 

1. A large open sketchbook page with a hand-drawn crest displays clear, legible text: "Source: Great-Aunt Elara’s 1920 Diary. Elements: Oak branch (resilience), River wave (origin). Note: These shapes are inherited memory. Do not alter the core geometry."
2. A tracing overlay with red ink annotations displays clear, legible text: "REVISION: Remove 'Star' symbol. No evidence in family records. Redraw border to match original curvature. Artist adds this flourish; it is not ancestral."
3. A white consent worksheet with a clear header and signature lines displays legible text: "Lineage Consent Form. I confirm the design respects our history. I authorize reproduction on skin only. No commercial use. Initials: ______ (Aunt) ______ (Client)"
4. A small label on the final stencil sheet displays legible text: "Stencil V2. Approved 14 Oct. For single use only. Do not distribute."

The artist points to a specific symbol on the tracing overlay, explaining it lacks historical basis. The aunt nods, confirming the removal. The artist then redraws the outer border to match the original sketch. Finally, both the aunt and the client pick up pens to initial the revised consent worksheet, authorizing the new design.

scene_type: documentary edit reconciles transcript, consent and narration
prompt_en: A documentary editing room at dusk. Two editors sit at a wide light table with a long column of paper transcript strips from an oral history. Beside the strips lie a narration draft page with a sentence circled in black ink, a small pink consent card from the narrator, and a spiral-bound ethical edit log. A clay bowl paperweight holds the strips open; red and blue pencils rest on a tray. Text on Transcript strip reads exactly: "MARTA: The neighbors said the bakery was haunted. They meant my grandmother sang after midnight in the flour room. It was the only hour the ovens were hers, and she sang the lullabies her mother brought from Tres Ríos. The singing was not a ghost. It was her remembering in the only place they let her work. When I tell this story, I want the oven hour, not the ghost.". Text on Narration draft page reads exactly: "NARRATION 7 DRAFT: The old bakery was haunted by a voice that came from nowhere, a ghost who sang before dawn. The sound was beautiful, and no one could explain it.". Text on Consent note card reads exactly: "I, Marta Reino, give permission for my words to be used only in full context and never arranged so they sound like someone else's story.". Text on Ethical edit log reads exactly: "EDIT LOG — Narration 7: removed 'a ghost who sang before dawn.' Marta's transcript, lines 12–14, shows the singing was her grandmother's memory of the ovens, not a specter. Restored the sentence 'It was her remembering in the only place they let her work.' Ask Marta to approve before the final cut.". One editor lifts the circled line from the narration draft and lays it over the transcript strip where the memory first appears. After reading the two texts together, the other editor draws a red line through the circled sentence, writes a dated note in the ethical edit log, and turns the consent card so its underlined condition faces the corrected strip.

scene_type: historic strike broadside rebuilt at a letterpress
prompt_en: A small union letterpress shop under lamplight. On the stone-topped table are a composing stick, loose metal sorts, a paper board holding a proof sheet, an open diary, and a press ledger. Racks of type rise behind the press; damp broadsheets hang from a line. An aproned printer and an apprentice work at the proofing press, oil and ink on their hands. Text on pinned proof sheet on wooden copyboard reads exactly: "THE WEAVERS' COVENANT. We, the hands of Marrow Mills, ask bread and rest. The loom stops until the pay book tells the truth.". Text on open diary page in ink handwriting reads exactly: "Etta Voss, 3 March. The committee accepted 'not one wheel turns.' Before dawn Krane warned; we softened it to 'the loom stops.' The truth stays here.". Text on open press ledger page reads exactly: "Ledger B-14. 12 March 1917: 300 copies. 100 to payroom, 200 to tenement gates. Paid 12 shillings reset type.". Text on pencil note pinned under the proof sheet reads exactly: "Later note by Silas Krane: The agent cut 'not one wheel turns' before the first pull. I kept the loom stops. Etta's diary is the true record.". The apprentice keeps the diary open while the printer places type in the composing stick. The printer lifts a pencil note from under the proof sheet, sets it beside the diary, checks the ledger entry, then turns the proof press. A clean sheet is lifted and read against the pinned proof.

prompt_en:
In a type-design studio, the late poet's adult daughter stands beside a designer at a long worktable. There are exactly two people in the scene. Open manuscript pages show the poet's handwriting; a large printed specimen of the new typeface lies near them. A postcard with a circled sketch of a lowercase g is propped beside the manuscripts, while a wall poster displays the typeface's current glyph variants and a proof sheet from the collected poems is prominently displayed on the table. The daughter notices that the printed specimen's g forms a conventional closed loop, unlike both the handwritten pages and the circled sketch. Text on Postcard message reads exactly: "Dear Mira, the small g I mean has an open, leaning tail, like a heron. Don't close the loop when you set my poems. E., Lisbon, 1968.". Text on Handwritten manuscript page reads exactly: "Morning, draft 3 (1974)
the small g leans into the next word
like a child at a window
and the morning keeps its breath". Text on Wall poster with glyph variants reads exactly: "Heron Type / Open g variants: 1968 postcard, 1974 draft, 1981 draft, 1986 diary, 1990 final". Text on Collected poems proof sheet reads exactly: "Collected Poems, p. 14, line 3, proof 2 sets g as closed loop. Compare 1974 manuscript, 1968 postcard. Correct g026 to open tail.". Text on Marginal annotation on corrected proof reads exactly: "Yes — this is it. Keep the open tail.". The designer compares the g forms on the manuscript, postcard, and poster, then revises the vector outline in the type-editing interface. After printing a corrected proof, the designer tapes it over the wall poster. The daughter checks the revised g against the postcard and writes a short annotation in the proof's margin.

scene_type: maritime logbook and signal flags resolve a rescue story
title_en: The Signal That Turned the Mabel H.
title_zh: 让“梅布尔号”转向的信号
prompt_en: In the low-ceiled workroom of a coastal heritage trust, two archivists and a retired pilot stand around a long oak table. One side holds an open signal-chest with rolled flags and cork floats; the table holds an open keeper's logbook surrounded by a code card, a typed letter, and a small chalkboard. A short halyard is strung across the room for indoor flag hoisting. The room smells faintly of tar, ink, and old paper. Text on open keeper's logbook reads exactly: "18 March 1937. South wind freshening, sea rough, glass falling. At 14:40 the coaster Mabel H. raised two flags close together: red over yellow, and a black square. I read red-over-yellow as a tow fault and answered with the storm cone. She wore north before dark came down. At 17:44 her mast light vanished under Gull Rock. I held to the old code and lost her. Keeper A. Calder.". Text on laminated code card reads exactly: "1912 Coast Code, Wreck Card No. 4 — hoist as one string, read lower flag first: red over yellow = boat disabled, require tow; black square = anchor dragging; storm cone = harbor closed, no entry.". Text on typed survivor's letter reads exactly: "Dear Mr. Calder, I am Elias Voss, mate of the Mabel H. My captain took your cone as a closed harbor and wore north. I knew the old card said red over yellow was disabled, not a tow fault. The card hung by the binnacle, but nobody touched it after 1930. I am sending you that page. We lost two men off Gull Rock. I do not blame you; I blame the years we trusted memory over the printed code. I hope the next keeper reads the card first. Respectfully, Elias Voss.". Text on small chalkboard reads exactly: "14:40 – Mabel H. hoists red/yellow + black square. 14:52 – storm cone raised. 15:10 – Mabel H. turns north. 17:44 – mast light lost. Corrected reading: red/yellow means disabled, cone should not have gone up.". One archivist points to a line in the open log, then turns the code card so its flag sequence faces up, and taps the typed letter. The retired pilot lifts two small folded signal flags from the chest, clips them to the indoor halyard, and raises them side by side. Another person erases one chalk line on the board and writes a fresh line above the old times. The visible writing reveals how the navigational mistake was read and corrected.

scene_type: costume atelier reconstructs an uncredited performer's coat
prompt_en: A small costume atelier in the late afternoon. On a dress form stands a worn burgundy velvet evening coat with one shoulder sitting slightly higher than the other. The worktable holds spread pattern paper with red pencil marks, an open ledger, a handwritten letter, and a small museum label. Measuring tape, shears, and spools of thread rest near the fabric shelves. Text on handwritten letter pinned beside the dress form reads exactly: "Dear Mrs. Hale, please keep the extra two inches at the shoulder and the deep side pocket for my script. I know the programme leaves me out, but the coat remembers. I wore it ninety-one times under the blue light. Yours, Elinor Voss.". Text on open wardrobe ledger page reads exactly: "Wardrobe Ledger 1937–38. Burgundy velvet coat — worn by Miss E. Voss, understudy, 91 performances. Altered: shoulder +2in, deep side pocket. No programme credit.". Text on red-pencil note on pattern paper reads exactly: "Add 2in to shoulder — E.V.". Text on corrected exhibition label reads exactly: "Evening coat. Worn by Elinor Voss, understudy at the Corinth Theatre, 1937–1938. She performed ninety-one nights; the coat is the archive the programme erased.". A costume maker lifts the folded letter from the coat's deep side pocket, reads it through, then checks the open ledger and measures the coat's shoulder against the pattern. She traces the red pencil note with her finger, nods, and fastens a corrected exhibition label to the lining.

scene_type: folk-dance phrase transmitted through floor marks and memory
title_en: The Quay That Changed the Step
prompt_en: A community hall with a worn wooden floor and folding chairs along one wall. A low stand stands beside a long chalk drawing on the floor; an open notebook rests on the stand, and a separate narrow rhythm card is taped strictly to the front edge of the stand. On the floor, chalk route labels and arrows mark two paths side by side; at the start of the route a small correction card is propped upright, showing only a version code and source line. An older teacher and three adult dancers in socks gather around the floor marks; the low stand is placed so the rhythm card and both chalk paths are visible together. Text on chalk route labels drawn on the wooden floor reads exactly: "OLD PATH — heel-cut step / NEW PATH — ball-lift step". Text on narrow rhythm-syllable card taped to the front edge of the low stand reads exactly: "bom · pa · TA-TA / soft · up · hold". Text on handwritten page in an open notebook resting on the low stand reads exactly: "When my mother left Fuen in the dry year, the ship's deck was too crowded for the heel-beat, so on the quay at Bruma she changed it to a soft ball step. She always said the sea gave the dance a new footfall. I teach the phrase as she passed it: quiet on the downbeat, lift on the turn.". Text on correction card propped upright at the start of the chalk route reads exactly: "LINE 6 / OLD HEEL-CUT = SHORE VERSION / B8 BALL-LIFT = HARBOR VERSION / SOURCE: ÁUREA MATOS, BRUMA, 1962". The teacher crouches and points at the correction card, then firmly stamps her heel into the wood to demonstrate the old footfall; immediately after, she repeats the phrase with a soft, distinct lift of her forefoot to demonstrate the new step. The three dancers watch her feet closely, glance at the narrow rhythm card on the stand, and follow the two chalk paths across the floor. One dancer touches the edge of the correction card while passing.

Mara Venn, the writer-artist, kneels by the board with a blue pencil; Jules Okonkwo, the letterer, sits at a low table with pens, brushes, a jar of ink, and sheets of translucent overlay paper. I found the key under the bridge, but the box smelled of harbor smoke. I am learning to read that smell.". Text on Mara's blue-pencil margin note beside the overlay reads exactly: "Move monologue to panel 6. Let panel 4 stay empty. Keep 'tin box' tight, let 'harbor smoke' be loose and low.". Mara crosses out an earlier line in the original word balloon with blue pencil and tapes Jules's revised overlay over the lower panel. Jules lifts the overlay, reads the monologue once, then adds a margin note about moving the text to a later panel. Mara nods, erases the old sound effect in the fourth panel, and watches Jules write the new onomatopoeia below it. Jules also attaches a separate slip with lettering instructions next to the monologue. Together they adjust the pacing by choosing which words stay tight and which are allowed to loosen.

In a softly lit animation archive, an archivist's bench holds a small stop-motion puppet of a young woman in a traveling coat, a miniature valise, a compartmentalized tray of numbered mouth shapes, a typed exposure sheet under a brass paperweight, and a faded letter flattened beside a small door model. ACTION: 'Left hand lifts the valise; right hand turns the latch.'

title_en: The Street That Held Two Names
prompt_en: In a bright community hall, five neighbors gather around a large printed street map spread across a worktable. The map is marked with numbered listening stations, a small printed route card clipped to its lower edge, and a handwritten field-note page set near the fourth station. A woman in a knitted vest gestures toward the alley; a man holds a coil of headphones, and a younger resident keeps a sticky note balanced on the map's edge. Text on handwritten field-note page set near the fourth station reads exactly: "At station 4 the fishmonger's bell calls the same hour my mother heard it in 1962. I stood at the corner and wrote the name from her mouth: Katel Alley, not Kettle. The kettle hiss was the tea shop vent.". Text on small printed route card clipped to the map's lower edge reads exactly: "Route: start at ST1 beside the bakery, pause at ST3 under the clock, finish where the alley stops sounding.". Text on printed station-label list along the map margin reads exactly: "ST1 bakery door • ST3 clock tower • ST4 fish bell, kettle hiss, iron grate • ST5 cart rattle". Text on handwritten sticky note balanced on the map's edge reads exactly: "The map printed one name, my neighbor heard another. I will trust her voice.". One resident pins the handwritten field note to the map. Another traces a penciled route line from the first station to the third and then pauses at the fourth, where the younger resident places the sticky note next to the printed place name. The group leans in as the older resident speaks.

scene_type: board-game club reconstructs rules from an incomplete set
title_en: The Missing Rule at the Long Table
prompt_en: Inside a wood-paneled community hall, a board-game club sits around a long table spread with a wool blanket. An open game box stands at one end; beside it lies the sea-map board with painted islands, wooden sailor tokens, small brass bells, and grey fog counters. Around the board are several paper documents: a torn printed booklet leaf, a handwritten house-rule scrap, a tournament record sheet, and a proposal card with pencil marks. Text on printed rule leaflet from the original game booklet reads exactly: "Rule 7 — The three lamps of Coracle Bell. They must be lit before dawn on the same island. If fog tokens outnumber the lamps, the sailor token is carried to the far reef. The crew loses one shared resource, and the story continues from the next year. The ferry token returns to the harbor at the turn after the rescue.". Text on handwritten scrap of paper reads exactly: "House rule, Red Lamp Club, 1979: if a page is missing, every player writes the number they remember. We keep the smallest number until the tournament sheet returns.". Text on carbon-copy tournament record sheet reads exactly: "North Harbor Tournament, 1988 — Round 4. Fog came before the third move. Judge Marta ruled from the missing page: count fog only after the third move, and one bell may be spent to see the tide map. Rescue cost was doubled.". Text on proposed reconstruction card reads exactly: "Proposed reconstruction — Rule 7a. Count fog only after the third move. A crew may spend one bell token to view the tide map before deciding. This follows the 1988 judge's record.". Text on pencil note on the reconstruction card reads exactly: "Accepted 4 Nov. — page 4 restored.". A player places the proposal card beside the printed booklet leaf and taps the tournament record sheet. Another player unfolds the handwritten house-rule scrap between them, comparing it with the proposal. The group sets three bell tokens on one painted island, then adds grey fog counters; when the grey counters overtake the bells, a player moves the wooden sailor token to a reef space. A fourth player writes an acceptance note on the proposal card, then tucks it back into the torn spine of the booklet.

scene_type: migrant diner memory reconstructed from menu and receipts
prompt_en: Inside a community hall, a temporary installation rebuilds the counter of a fictional all-night diner. A worn wooden counter, chrome stools, a chalkboard menu on a stand, a corkboard holding a letter and receipts, and a glass case containing one small pale-purple yam tuber with smooth, firm skin and no branching rootlets. Two former customers sit at the counter with their coats on; a retired cook in a stained apron stands behind it. Penciled index cards are taped near a napkin dispenser, and a shoe box holds more cards. A small basket on the counter holds several more dry pale-purple yam tubers, the same compact, smooth-skinned shape as the specimen under glass. A single warm lamp casts a pool of light across the counter. Text on a handwritten letter pinned to a corkboard, written on lined notebook paper reads exactly: "I am from a tin town. At Mariam's stall I found a pale purple root and remembered my aunt's yam soup. I bought a sack. My first customers wrinkled their noses. I roasted it with garlic and palm oil, and by spring everyone ordered Quiet Root Stew, though the true name was still unknown.". Text on a small brown-paper receipt pinned beside the letter, with torn perforated edge reads exactly: "MARIAM'S TROPICAL PROVISIONS — 18 JAN 1988 / 2 sacks purple yams, 14 lb / 1 bottle palm oil / 5 lb chickpeas / bitter greens / total $11.20 — PAID". Text on a chalkboard menu standing on the counter, with a handwritten correction over the first line reads exactly: "HAN'S LATE NIGHT / WINTER 1988 / Quiet Root Stew over rice — $3.50 / Fish sauce eggs — $2.00 / Bitter greens with garlic — $1.75 / Tea, always free". Text on an index card taped above the napkin dispenser, handwriting in pencil reads exactly: "Every Tuesday after the 4 a.m. streetcar I ate the stew. It tasted like my grandmother's mountain. Years later Mariam's stall had a paper sign: 'Lila yam from the highlands.' That is how the root got its true name.". The retired cook pins the supplier receipt beside a handwritten letter on the corkboard, then turns the chalkboard menu so the patrons can read it. One patron points at the menu, picks up an index card taped above the napkin dispenser, and reads it. The other patron pulls a paper sign from the shoe box that gives the root's later name, places a small basket of pale-purple yam tubers on the counter, and aligns one compact pale-purple tuber with the paper sign and the brown-paper receipt. The cook nods and adds a penciled note to the menu's first line.

scene_type: book repair traces a volume through ownership inscriptions
title_en: The Coast Road in the Endpapers
prompt_en: An open travel volume rests on a padded cradle on a conservator's workbench. The front flyleaf carries a dark ink passage with a paler pencil reply beneath it; near the spine fold lies a loose page section. A needle and thread lie on the bench beside a stack of blank repair labels. Text on Front flyleaf of the travel volume reads exactly: "Perla Navarre bought this book in Torremuelle on 14 May 1932, the day the mule road washed out. I carried it over the cliff stair to Serpent Bay and read it aloud to my father, who had walked the same coast forty years earlier. He laughed at the compass sketch, saying the iron fence was never there. I keep it because the route is already changing and the book will know what I remembered.". Text on Margin below the first-owner passage, same flyleaf reads exactly: "R. March, 1961: The cliff stair is a rubble line now. I walked it with the book in hand, and found the iron fence just as she remembered, hidden under blackberry. The old name was Ciego Gate.". Text on Pasted slip in the rear pastedown reads exactly: "Merrow Public Library. Accession 4417. Gift of Ruth March, 1963. Shelved Travel, Case 9. Inscribed 'not to be lent.'". Text on Tipped-in repair label near the spine fold reads exactly: "Conservation repair by Tamsin Voss, July 1984. Re-sewn through three signatures. Removed adhesive tape from the facing page. All ink inscriptions preserved.". The conservator tilts the flyleaf toward the lamp to follow the ink passage, then the pencil reply. She checks the printed accession slip in the rear pastedown, returns the loose pages to their original order, and sews through the first signature. She then writes a dated repair label and sets it beside the book.

scene_type: illustrated story scroll unfolds during oral narration
title_en: The Scroll That Lets the Smallest Ask
title_zh: 让最小的孩子先问的画卷
prompt_en: In a lamplit reading room of a small harbor library, an elderly storyteller and a younger illustrator unroll a long painted paper scroll across a low oak table. A small audience sits on cushions and stools around the table. The scroll has hand-painted panels with short ink labels, and a red ribbon bearing a repeated line hangs from one edge. A folded paper note rests inside the scroll's wooden case. Text on folded note kept inside the scroll case reads exactly: "Keep the ending light. In 1962 old Marta added a white fish and the children would not sleep until it returned. The river must give it back. Told this rule to Nor, then to me. Pass it on, but let the smallest listener ask first.". Text on ink label above a painted scroll panel reads exactly: "The goose rings the wet bell.". Text on ink label above the willow panel reads exactly: "The white fish waits under the willow.". Text on red ribbon stitched near the scroll's lower edge reads exactly: "The river answered, again, again.". Text on folded crayon note handed up by a child reads exactly: "If the goose rang the bell, did the white fish hear it above the river?". The storyteller lifts the folded note from the scroll case as the illustrator holds the far edge of the paper. She reads it aloud, then slides a finger along the painted panels, pausing at the scene where a waterbird faces a hanging bell and again where a pale fish passes beneath a willow. She resumes the tale in rhythm, flicking the refrain ribbon so it sways. A child in the audience writes on a scrap of paper, folds it, and hands it up. The storyteller reads the question, smiles, and tucks the note under the ribbon at the very end of the scroll, where the last panel is still blank.

title_en: The Lake Kept Every Wrong Turn

prompt_en: Two old friends sit at a kitchen table with a cassette deck, a typewritten liner note, an open spiral notebook full of song titles, a faded postcard, and a newer index card. A half-empty mug and a pen lie between them; the deck door is open and a cassette sits on the table. Text on typewritten J-card liner note reads exactly: "Lake House, 1994. The lake kept every wrong turn. You hid the oars because you were not ready to leave. I called it a lie, so you mailed me the date I refused. Play side B loud. The hiss is the water we almost lost.". Text on handwritten tracklist in spiral notebook reads exactly: "Side A: Salt on the Porch — we cracked the porch light; The Bee Line; Lantern Logic. Side B: Almost-Float; The Postcard That Lied — because the date was wrong.". Text on faded postcard reads exactly: "August 1 — I hid the oars. Not gone. Love, Lena". Text on new index-card note reads exactly: "Found the oars under the porch. The card was sent July 30 but dated Aug. 1.". Mira turns the postcard over and taps the postmark, then slides the index card to Lena. Lena reads it, compares the tracklist's last song title with the postcard, and pencils the true postmark date onto the back of the postcard. The cassette begins to play, and the two friends lean toward the speaker without speaking.

scene_type: procession banner repair records a community's changing names
title_en: The Banner Under Every Added Name
title_zh: 在每一个增添的名字下
prompt_en: Inside an enclosed upstairs community textile conservation room, four solid walls, a closed door, and a tall window separate the work space from the narrow street outside; through the window the street can be seen far below and never enters the room. A long worktable stands indoors below the window under a warm work lamp, holding three distinct text carriers: a scarlet processional banner spread flat for repair, an open steward's repair ledger set beside it, and a small route card tucked between the ledger's pages. A fourth carrier, an unstitched cloth patch, is held in a volunteer's hand above the banner's lower hem. The banner's stacked gold-thread embroidery records different group names from different decades, with each newer line sewn below the older ones, showing a collective history of names being added rather than erased. Text on Scarlet processional banner spread flat on the indoor worktable, with stacked gold-thread embroidery on scarlet cotton reads exactly: "Lantern Bearers of Eastbrook 1927 · Eastbrook Neighbors' Procession 1948 · United Lantern Fellowship 1961 · Eastbrook Lantern Walkers 1975". Text on Steward's repair ledger, open page lying on the indoor table beside the banner reads exactly: "When the weaving families left in 1961, the mill hands did not ask to replace the banner by force. They asked to be added under a truthful name. I crossed out nothing; I wrote 'Eastbrook Lantern Walkers' below the old line, and every route since has ended at Every Door.". Text on Route card tucked between the pages of the open repair ledger reads exactly: "1927 Night Lane–Quarry Gate · 1948 Night Lane–Mill Bridge · 1961 Night Lane–Weaver's Cross · 1975 Night Lane–Every Door". Text on Unstitched patch held in a volunteer's hand above the banner's lower hem reads exactly: "All who walk may carry the light". Volunteers sit around the indoor long table, keeping the scarlet banner spread flat while they repair it. One volunteer sets the open account book beside the banner so the steward's handwritten record lies under the oldest stitched line. Another volunteer draws a threaded needle through the lower hem and fixes the welcome patch below the newest embroidered name. title_en: The Lane Takes Shape at the Table
prompt_en: In a community room beside a closed library, a long table holds a low plywood model of a demolished street block. Photocopied clearance photos and a captioned planning strip lie near the edge. A handwritten index card is propped against a small cardboard bakery with a green door. A blue-pencil route loops across the painted road. Residents of different ages stand around the table, some holding toothpick labels, one adjusting a miniature fig tree in a cardboard yard. Text on handwritten index card propped against the miniature bakery reads exactly: "At No. 14 Bellwether Lane, my mother ran a bakery behind a green tin door. The alley smelled of rosemary, not oil. We sold seeded rye and kept the ovens going until the last train sounded. The Harrowgate file calls the building vacant, but I keep the ledger pages: rye, milk bread, burnt honey cake. My father weighed flour on brass scales, and the back yard had a fig tree. The window seat over the counter looked all the way down the lane, and every evening the bakery cat waited by the door.". Text on typed caption strip taped beneath a photocopied clearance photograph reads exactly: "Harrowgate Planning Office, clearance file C-118. Bellwether Lane block, surveyed June 1992. No. 12–18 vacant; no commercial use recorded at No. 14; site listed as storage.". Text on inked paper tape laid along the model edge reads exactly: "Grandmother at No. 16 Bellwether sent me to the bakery before dusk. I counted seven paces to the green door at No. 14, crossed to avoid the crack at No. 15, rang the bell at No. 18, and carried a warm heel of rye home. I wrote this in 2019 for the Bellwether Remembered box.". Text on toothpick label flags standing in the model reads exactly: "14 Green Door Bakery · 15 Colm & Sons · 16 Cho House · 18 Night Bell Repair". Text on small cardboard sign taped to the table skirt reads exactly: "Bellwether Remembered workshop — this model is a shared memory, not an official map.". An older resident lifts the miniature bakery from the wrong doorway and sets it at number fourteen, then presses it down so it meets the painted blue route. A younger resident taps the official caption strip, then the index card, and shrugs. Another resident writes a fresh label and pushes it into the base of the corner house. The group moves a tiny fig tree into the back yard, and someone turns the clearance photocopy face down beside the model.

prompt_en:
At a letterpress proofing table, a blind poet reads an embossed sheet with both hands while a printer aligns a translucent print overlay above the same lines. not commas, before the shore answers.
— poem by Lena Marr". Text on tactile line-four proof strip beside the poet's left hand, rendered with visible braille dots and raised texture, reads exactly: "LINE 4 CELLS

title_en: The Catch That Took the Bow
prompt_en: A single continuous rehearsal room holds a worn illusion cabinet with its door swung open and a wooden worktable beside it. Stage magician Calder Vale stands at the open cabinet door; prop maker Mara Osei stands at the same worktable. A brass-framed card is fixed to the outside of the cabinet door, an open working notebook lies on the table, a penciled inscription runs along an inner wooden slat of the cabinet, and a small printed attribution card is at the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame. Text on brass-framed patter card fixed to the outside of the cabinet door reads exactly: "Tonight, my own invention — The Vanishing Wardrobe — a mystery I built with my own hands.". Text on open working notebook on the wooden worktable reads exactly: "Cabinet constructed by Mara Osei, mechanic, 1948. Calder wrote the script, chose the silk, and took the bows. The hinge pivot and catch that make the vanish possible were Osei's. Public credit never matched the work.". Text on inner wooden slat of the cabinet beside the hinge pivot reads exactly: "OS-WARD-48 / pivot no.3 / oil before cue / silent count of seven.". Text on small printed attribution card slipped into the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame reads exactly: "The Vanishing Wardrobe. Devised by Calder Vale and Mara Osei. Illusion mechanism designed and built by Mara Osei, 1948.". The prop maker turns a page of the working notebook on the table, taps a penciled correction in the margin, then slides a small printed attribution card into the pocket on the cabinet's inner frame. The stage magician holds the cabinet door open, turns his gaze from the notebook to the card, and faces the revised credit statement in the same continuous room.

scene_type: tabletop role-playing campaign archive becomes collective literature
prompt_en: In a small bindery at night, a single long archive table stands under one work lamp, its surface unbroken from one end to the other. Four distinguishable players sit around that same table: a grey-haired woman at the left, a bearded man across from her, a bespectacled younger woman at the right, and a man with rolled sleeves at the far end. The shared tabletop holds, together in one plane, a large hand-drawn fantasy map weighted by a brass handbell and a flat stone; an open campaign chronicle with a mounted old paper letter on its left page and a ruled session record on its right page; a few loose journal pages beside the book; and a hand-sewn chapbook lying open next to the chronicle with its title page facing up. Nothing on the table is separated into frames, stands, or separate display cells. Text on aged paper letter mounted inside the left page of the open campaign chronicle reads exactly: "Mireva of the Ash-Road, to the cartographers who crossed after the flood. The bell proved you were there, and the old ledger was wrong, not the river.". Text on ruled session entry on the right page of the same open campaign chronicle reads exactly: "Session 14 / Graywater Bridge / Watch 11 / Bell rang once / Ferry carried four / No roll defeated the river.". Text on margin of the same right page, written in two ink colors reads exactly: "Ari wrote: “the bridge fell at dawn.” I wrote back: “No, the ledger failed.”". Text on title page of a hand-sewn chapbook lying open beside the campaign chronicle reads exactly: "The Thornfoot Epilogue — Four hands, one river.". The grey-haired woman flips the campaign chronicle to the page with the mounted letter and sets the flat stone on the letter. The bearded man writes a short correction with a second ink color in the margin beside the ruled session entry. The bespectacled younger woman touches that margin correction with a fingertip, then points to the closing line of the mounted letter. The man with rolled sleeves lifts the hand-sewn chapbook, turns its title page toward the lamp, reads it, and puts it back beside the open chronicle on the same tabletop.

In a quiet study room with paper scrolls hanging on the walls, a young student stands beside a low wooden table. On the table lies a large sheet of xuan paper with rows of Chinese characters written by the student. An older teacher, holding a brush dipped in red ink, leans over the sheet, about to make annotations. The room is lit by warm light from a paper lantern, and other practice sheets are stacked to the side. Text on Student practice sheet reads exactly: "永和九年，岁在癸丑，暮春之初，会于会稽山阴之兰亭，修禊事也。
暮春者，春服既成，冠者五六人，童子六七人，浴乎沂，风乎舞雩，咏而归。
右军此帖，气韵生动，笔势遒媚。余今晨临摹三遍，觉其转折处尚欠圆融。夫子尝言，学书先贵立品，品高则笔自雅。吾当勤习永字八法，以求笔笔中锋。
余细观此帖，羲之运笔如行云流水。今所临“永”字，点画尚欠精到。录其要旨：永字八法者，点为侧，横为勒，竖为努，钩为趯，提为策，撇为掠，短撇为啄，捺为磔。书时须心正笔正，落纸云烟，勿使笔毫散乱。
今临至“惠风和畅”，觉其行气贯通，然“畅”字之撇捺尚觉滞涩。取张怀瓘《书断》所言“笔断意连”之旨，当以虚引实，方得右军之韵。". Text on Teacher's red annotation on margin reads exactly: "此字中锋圆劲，然提按不足，王体精髓在腕活。
用笔之法，贵在藏锋。此字起笔宜逆入平出，收笔回锋。
另：此字戈法稍弱，出钩宜蓄势上挑，如长空新月。
此数字中锋尚可，然牵丝处欠虚灵。王字贵在映带左右，行气一贯。尔临兰亭，当先求形似，后追神韵。留意其藏锋、逆势、回锋诸法，日课不辍，方有所成。". Text on Model inscription hanging on wall reads exactly: "兰亭序·神龙本
临此本需参以冯承素摹本，细察牵丝映带。
神龙本为唐摹，钩摹精细，锋芒毕现。临写时须观其起收笔势，仿其牵丝映带，不可失其风神。
冯摹本中锋转折处最见功力，临写时须留意提按缓急。". The teacher points to a specific character on the student's sheet, then writes a small annotation in red ink beside it. He then gestures to a model inscription hanging on the wall, explaining a historical stroke pattern. The student nods while holding a brush.
